items.note: Udaipur and Patari in Vidisha district are rich in stone quarries; the stone is cut and exported abroad.
items.gloss: Udaipur and Patari in Vidisha district are an area made rich by stone quarries. The stone here, after being cut and dressed, is sent abroad.

items.note: Author's estimate of over a hundred crorepati traders in cloth, grain and stone nearby (Ganj Basoda), able to raise crores for Udaypur's development.
items.gloss: There must be over a hundred crorepati traders in cloth, grain and stone. If a collector spread his bag for Udaipur's development, raising two or four crore in a single meeting would not be hard.

reject_reason: anecdote about officials; no evidence on Udaypur
journalistic comparison with Bakhtiyarpur; no Udaypur evidence

items.note: Bijamandal-like building in a residential complex, of the temple's time, with an incomplete inscription, temple-like doorway, pillars and sanctum, used for cattle and fodder.
items.gloss: First ask someone for the Bijamandal: a building in a residential complex, made in the time of the temple, with an incomplete inscription, a temple-like entrance, pillars and a sanctum. Here you will find cattle tied and fodder stored.

items.note: Jain temple complex with Tirthankara images mutilated at some time; broken images as old as Udaypur's history.
items.gloss: Ask someone for the Jain temple complex. There the weaponless Tirthankaras have waited for you for decades, their images having been struck at some period. Their broken images are as old as the history of Udaipur.

items.note: Author infers Jain followers existed in Udaypur since such grand images needed patrons; not a city only of Shiva worshippers.
items.gloss: Their broken images are as old as Udaipur's history. This was not only a city of Shiva worshippers; there must have been many followers of the Tirthankaras, otherwise who would have commissioned such grand images?

items.note: Pisanhari's simple temple, with a doorway of matchless carving.
items.gloss: Anyone can tell you of Pisanhari's plain temple, built very simply. But the splendid carving of its entrance is unmatched.

items.note: Niches in palace-ruin doors and walls show Paramara design; stone walls raised between corridor pillars are later occupation.
items.gloss: The niches surviving in their doors and walls are a splendid display of Paramara design. Stone walls raised between the pillars of the corridors will tell you plainly that these are encroachments of a later period.

items.note: Population of eight thousand with one to one-and-a-half thousand Muslims; author says their ancestors helped shape the town in Udayaditya's time.
items.gloss: Of a population of eight thousand, one to one and a half thousand are Muslims. But in the time of Paramara king Udayaditya their ancestors were the people who shaped this town: some craftsman, guard, trader, courtier or priest. Identity was broken like the images.

items.note: Devi temple on Ghatera road with a stepwell like Vidisha's Bijamandal; recent excavation found an older stepwell with a 45-degree ramp.
items.gloss: On Ghatera Road is a devi temple where you will see a stepwell exactly like the Bijamandal of Vidisha, and several broken images. A recent mound excavation found an older stepwell with a 45-degree ramp going below ground level. People must once have gone straight down; horses descended by it.

items.note: Linga-shaped block cut from the hill read as an unfinished Paramara rock temple, with images being carved on the cut hill.
items.gloss: A piece cut from the original mountain, shaped like a Shivalinga, is visible from miles away. It is a very unfinished Paramara-period rock temple that was never completed. Images were being carved on that cut hill; the project must have stopped for some reason.

items.note: Remains of fort ramparts on hill paths bear centuries of witness.
items.gloss: On the hill paths, remains of the fort ramparts look angry because no one comes to see them. They hold centuries of testimony.

items.note: Large old stone gateways set along roads in the Paramara town; rows of shops beside them filled with debris, perhaps part of a lively bazaar.
items.gloss: Walking the lanes you pass through large old stone gateways. In the orderly Paramara Udaipur these gates were set across roads. Beside them are rows of shops filled with centuries of debris; they must have been part of a lively market.

items.note: Old houses turning to rubble, with courtyards, rooms and verandas of big houses whose owners and abandonment are unknown.
items.gloss: Many old houses are turning into debris. Climbing a heap and peering in, you see courtyards, rooms and verandas. Special people must have lived in these big houses. Who were they, when were these splendid homes abandoned, and who is the heir today?

items.note: Author asks how the temple survived when Vijay Mandir did not, suggesting organised local resistance meant only the images were broken (conjecture).
items.gloss: The question must arise: how did this temple survive? Who stopped it from sharing the fate of Vidisha's Bijamandal? Was it because of organised resistance by Udaipur's local people that only the images could be broken and the raiders were driven off?

items.note: Several 800-900 year old inscriptions on both sides of each doorway include Maharaj Udayaditya's name.
items.gloss: Entering the sanctum last through any door, you will find on both sides several inscriptions eight to nine hundred years old. Among them you will find the name of Maharaj Udayaditya too.

items.note: Inscriptions 800-900 years old at the doorways bear Udayaditya's name; images broken deep inside.
items.gloss: Entering the sanctum last through any door, you find on both sides many inscriptions eight to nine hundred years old. Maharaj Udayaditya's name is among them. Images were broken even inside.

items.note: Visitor's pledge: preserve ancestors' remaining heritage, awaken local people, face true history.
items.gloss: Leave with some resolve: a resolve to preserve the remnants of our great ancestors' heritage, to awaken the people around, and to face true history.

reject_reason: exhortation listing other sites; no Udaypur evidence

items.note: Reporter Govind Saxena cycled 70 km to Udaypur and filmed the palace's verandas, halls, stairs and cellars; the rooftop held as private property now padlocked.
items.gloss: Govind Saxena came to Udaipur one day by bike over 70 kilometres. He went into many ruined verandas, deserted halls, dusty stairs and torn-up cellars and filmed the palace from every angle. He also went to the roof that had been kept as private property, now locked with a large iron gate.

reject_reason: pilot-judged for C01; nothing for C02–C13
reporter's diary detail; no evidence for any unit

items.note: Describes Udayaditya as Bhoja's successor who added lustre to Paramara achievement.
items.gloss: This is the story of the great works of the Paramara kings, to whose glory Udayaditya, a successor of King Bhoja, added lustre.

items.note: Palace passed to plunderers; Qazi identity; an archaeology department functionary sees only Mughal and Mandu sultan contributions, not the founding.
items.gloss: Maharaj Udayaditya's palace too fell into the hands of plunderers in later centuries. New identities emerged under the name of Qazi. Govind is astonished that an archaeology department official, Ahmad Ali, sees in this Paramara town only the Mughals' and Mandu sultans' encroachment as contribution, not seeing beyond the Mughals to when the town was settled and the temple and palace built.

items.note: A one-page 2008 Hindi translation of a Persian original, presented before the tehsildar, was sent to the author; basis of the Babur prayer farman discussion.
items.gloss: An official said a one-page document had been presented by a lawyer before the tehsildar. It was also sent to me by an officer. It was a Hindi translation, made in 2008, of some original Persian text.

items.note: Within two weeks the unlawful occupiers of the ancient palace ruins left, handing the keys to officials.
items.gloss: It is no small relief that in a very fast action in just two weeks, illegal occupiers have been removed from the ruins of Udaipur's ancient palace. Rather, the occupiers themselves left, handing the keys to officials.

items.note: Four to five centuries after Udayaditya Udaypur continued but as a neglected town in Chanderi suba, per the Persian farman.
items.gloss: It is certain that four-five centuries after Maharaj Udayaditya Udaipur's existence continued but it had become a neglected faraway town, part of the Chanderi province. This is what the Persian farman says.

items.note: The farman's phrase 'Firdaus Makani' explained as an honorific title of Babur.
items.gloss: Know that this is the respectful title of the Mughal invader Babur. Firdaus Makani means one whose house is in paradise; Firdaus means paradise.

items.note: Udaypur's fate no longer in Paramara hands; more than 300 years since they left history; linked to Chanderi.
items.gloss: Udaipur's fortune-makers were no longer the Paramaras. More than three hundred years had passed since the Paramaras departed from history. Udaipur's connection was now with Chanderi.

reject_reason: general commentary on jauhar; no Udaypur evidence

items.note: Chanderi Darwaza: a gate in the Udaypur fort wall parallel to the main road, on the north side, named for the town it faces.
items.gloss: Bad news of that great massacre must have come to Udaipur through the Chanderi gate. It is a gate of Udaipur's fort wall running parallel to the main road, on the north side. In that era a city's gate was named for the big city it faced.

items.note: Per the farman, a mosque was built at Udaypur in Jahangir's time and worshippers ordered to pray for Babur and Shah Jahan.
items.gloss: Paramara Udaipur appears as a remote town stuck in Chanderi province, where according to this farman a mosque was built in the time of Jahangir. Worshippers in the mosque are now ordered to remember Babur with a fatiha prayer. The present emperor too is to be prayed for, that is, Babur and Shah Jahan together.

reject_reason: polemical commentary on conversion; no citable evidence

items.note: Oldest Paramara record from Udaypur is dated 1080; another of 1229 is of Devapaladeva.
items.gloss: The oldest record about Paramara kings obtained from Udaipur is of the year 1080 and another is of 1229, which is of Devapaladeva.

items.note: In Devapaladeva's time Iltutmish plundered Vidisha and Ujjain, the region's first Islamic contact.
items.gloss: In Devapaladeva's time Shamsuddin Iltutmish plundered Vidisha and Ujjain and badly ruined them. His raiding armies devastated all of Malwa in one long campaign. It was the first Islamic contact of this region.

items.note: Paramara splendour ended at Mandu by a force sent by Alauddin Khilji; King Mahlakdeva.
items.gloss: In time Paramara splendour ended at Mandu at the hands of a raiding band sent by Alauddin Khilji. That was Maharaj Mahlakdeva, who clashed with the Khiljis' storms. We do not know how many of his family were killed, how many survived and where they went.
